dm-weyl.title: The Weyl algebra and D-modules on affine space

questions.q: In the Weyl algebra $D_1 = \mathbb{C}\langle x, \partial \rangle / ([\partial, x] - 1)$, what is $\partial \cdot x^n$ as an element written in the standard basis $\{x^a \partial^b\}$ (powers of $x$ on the left)?
questions.explain: The defining relation $\partial x = x \partial + 1$ propagates by induction: $\partial x^n = (x\partial + 1) x^{n-1} = x \partial x^{n-1} + x^{n-1}$, and unwinding gives $\partial x^n = x^n \partial + n x^{n-1}$. This is exactly the product rule $\partial(x^n f) = n x^{n-1} f + x^n \partial f$ written in the algebra: the $n x^{n-1}$ term comes from differentiating $x^n$, the $x^n \partial$ term from leaving it alone.
questions.hint: Apply $[\partial, x] = 1$ repeatedly. Equivalently, what is the product rule for $\partial(x^n \cdot u)$?

questions.q: Which of the following is a $D_1$-module structure on $\mathbb{C}[x]$?
questions.explain: The standard action: $x$ acts by multiplication, $\partial$ acts by differentiation. The relation $[\partial, x] = 1$ is satisfied because $(\partial x - x \partial) f = (xf)' - x f' = f$. Option 4 also satisfies a commutation relation, but $[\partial, x] = x \cdot xf - x \cdot xf = 0 \ne 1$, so it is not a $D_1$-module. As a $D_1$-module, $\mathbb{C}[x] \cong D_1 / D_1 \cdot \partial$ — cyclic, generated by $1$.
questions.hint: Plug into the commutator relation $[\partial, x] = 1$ and check.

questions.q: Compute the dimension of the associated graded $\mathrm{gr}^F D_n$ in degree $k$, where $F^\bullet$ is the Bernstein filtration on the $n$-th Weyl algebra.
questions.explain: Because $\mathrm{gr}^F D_n = \mathbb{C}[x_1, \ldots, x_n, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_n]$ as a graded ring (a polynomial ring in $2n$ variables), its degree-$k$ piece is the space of homogeneous polynomials of total degree $k$ in $2n$ variables. That has dimension $\binom{k + 2n - 1}{2n - 1}$ — the standard 'stars and bars' count. Note $\dim \mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{gr}^F D_n) = 2n = \dim T^*\mathbb{A}^n$, the cotangent bundle of affine space.
questions.hint: $\mathrm{gr}^F D_n$ is the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[x_1, \ldots, x_n, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_n]$ — count monomials of total degree $k$ in $2n$ variables.

questions.q: Which equivalent description of an $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent $\mathcal{D}_X$-module on a smooth variety $X$ is correct?
choices: An $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent module $E$ together with a flat connection $\nabla : E \to E \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \Omega^1_X$ (i.e. $\mathbb{C}$-linear, Leibniz, $\nabla^2 = 0$).
An $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent module with the trivial $\mathcal{D}_X$-action $\partial \cdot m = 0$.
A locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$-module of finite rank, with no further structure.
An ideal sheaf $I \subset \mathcal{D}_X$ such that $\mathcal{D}_X / I$ is coherent.
questions.explain: On a smooth variety, $\mathcal{D}_X^{\le 1} = \mathcal{O}_X \oplus \mathcal{T}_X$ (vector fields) generates $\mathcal{D}_X$ over $\mathcal{O}_X$. So a $\mathcal{D}_X$-action restricts to a $\mathcal{T}_X$-action, i.e. a connection $\nabla$, and the relation $[\partial_i, \partial_j] = 0$ in $\mathcal{D}_X$ forces $\nabla^2 = 0$ — flatness. An $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent module need not be locally free (option 3 is too restrictive: skyscrapers are coherent), and option 2 is the constant connection on $\mathcal{O}_X$, only one example.
questions.hint: First-order operators are vector fields. What does giving an action of $\mathcal{T}_X$ mean for a sheaf on a smooth variety?

questions.q: On $X = \mathbb{A}^1$, consider $M = \mathcal{D} / \mathcal{D} \cdot x$ — the delta-function module. What is its rank as an $\mathcal{O}_X$-module on the open set $X \setminus \{0\}$?
questions.explain: On $X \setminus \{0\}$ the function $x$ is invertible, so the relation $x \cdot 1 = 0$ in $M$ forces $1 = 0$ on this open set — equivalently, $M|_{X \setminus \{0\}} = 0$. The module $\delta_0$ is supported on the single point $\{0\}$. As a $\mathcal{D}$-module on $\mathbb{A}^1$ it is non-zero but has rank $0$ over $\mathcal{O}_X$ generically; over $\mathbb{C}$ it is the infinite-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}\langle \delta, \partial \delta, \partial^2 \delta, \ldots \rangle$. This is the classic 'small as $\mathcal{D}$, big as $\mathbb{C}$' phenomenon.
questions.hint: $\delta_0$ is supported at the origin. What does that mean for its restriction to $X \setminus \{0\}$?

questions.q: For a closed embedding $i : Z \hookrightarrow X$ of smooth varieties, Kashiwara's theorem says $i_+ : \mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal{D}_Z) \to \mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal{D}_X)$ is fully faithful, with essential image those $\mathcal{D}_X$-modules supported (set-theoretically) on $Z$. What does the simplest case $Z = \{0\} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^1 = X$ say?
choices: Every $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbb{A}^1}$-module supported at $0$ is a (finite or infinite) direct sum of copies of the delta-module $\delta_0$.
The constant sheaf $\mathbb{C}$ on $\{0\}$ is the same as the constant sheaf on $\mathbb{A}^1$.
The functor $i_+$ is exact and never has higher derived functors.
questions.explain: $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal{D}_Z)$ for $Z$ a single point is the category of $\mathbb{C}$-vector spaces. Kashiwara's equivalence sends a vector space $V$ to $i_+ V = V \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} \delta_0$, and asserts every $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbb{A}^1}$-module supported at $0$ has this form — i.e. is a direct sum of copies of $\delta_0$. This is a strong rigidity statement: there is no 'nilpotent thickening' of $\delta_0$ as a coherent $\mathcal{D}$-module, in stark contrast to coherent $\mathcal{O}$-modules supported at $0$ (which include $\mathcal{O}/(x^k)$ for every $k$).
questions.hint: $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pt}})$ is the category of $\mathbb{C}$-vector spaces. What does Kashiwara's theorem then say about $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbb{A}^1}$-modules supported at $\{0\}$?

questions.q: On $X = \mathbb{A}^1$, what is the characteristic variety of $M = \delta_0 = \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D} \cdot x$ as a subset of $T^*X = \mathbb{A}^2_{x, \xi}$?
questions.explain: Take the Bernstein filtration $F^k M = $ image of $F^k \mathcal{D}$ in $M$. Then $\mathrm{gr}^F M \cong \mathbb{C}[\xi]$ as a graded module, with the relation $x \cdot 1 = 0$ becoming $x \cdot \xi^k = 0$ in the symbol algebra $\mathbb{C}[x, \xi]$. So $\mathrm{gr}^F M = \mathbb{C}[x, \xi] / (x) = \mathbb{C}[\xi]$, supported on $\{x = 0\}$ — the cotangent fibre at the origin. This is a Lagrangian line in $T^*\mathbb{A}^1$, so $\delta_0$ is holonomic.
questions.hint: $M$ is generated by $1$ subject to $x \cdot 1 = 0$. Pass to symbols: what relation does $\mathrm{gr}^F M$ satisfy in $\mathbb{C}[x, \xi]$?

questions.q: Bernstein's inequality says: for a non-zero coherent $\mathcal{D}_X$-module $M$ on a smooth $X$ of dimension $n$, every component of $\mathrm{Char}(M)$ has dimension $\ge n$. Why does involutivity of the characteristic ideal give this lower bound?
choices: Because $T^*X$ has dimension $2n$ and the symplectic form forces involutive subvarieties to have dimension $\ge n$.
Because every algebraic variety in $T^*X$ has dimension $\ge n$.
Because the inequality is a topological feature of the underlying space $X$, independent of the symplectic structure.
questions.explain: $T^*X$ carries the canonical symplectic form $\omega = \sum d\xi_i \wedge dx_i$, hence the Poisson bracket $\{f, g\}$ on $\mathbb{C}[T^*X]$. Gabber's theorem (1981) says the radical of $\mathrm{ann}(\mathrm{gr}^F M)$ is closed under the Poisson bracket — i.e. $\mathrm{Char}(M)$ is a coisotropic, hence involutive, subvariety of $T^*X$. A general fact in symplectic geometry: an involutive subvariety of a $2n$-dimensional symplectic variety has dimension at least $n$. The lower bound is sharp, achieved by holonomic modules (Lagrangian = involutive of minimal dimension).
questions.hint: Recall: involutive (= coisotropic) subvarieties of a symplectic $2n$-fold have dimension $\ge n$, with equality giving Lagrangians.

questions.q: On $X = \mathbb{A}^2$, which of the following coherent $\mathcal{D}_X$-modules is NOT holonomic?
choices: $\mathcal{O}_X$ — the structure sheaf with its tautological connection.
$\delta_{(0,0)} = \mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}(x_1, x_2)$ — the delta-module at the origin.
Any of the above can be holonomic, depending on convention.
questions.explain: Pass to symbols: $\mathrm{Char}(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}\partial_1) = V(\xi_1) \subset T^*\mathbb{A}^2$, which is a hypersurface of dimension $3$ in the $4$-dimensional cotangent bundle. Bernstein's bound is $\dim \ge 2$ — satisfied — but holonomicity demands $\dim = 2$ exactly, which fails here. The module $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}\partial_1$ is a 'partial' system: it imposes one PDE $\partial_1 u = 0$ on a function of two variables, giving a one-parameter family of solutions $u = u(x_2)$. Two PDEs (e.g. $\partial_1 u = \partial_2 u = 0$) are needed to cut down to a finite-dimensional solution space, i.e. holonomicity.
questions.hint: Compute the characteristic variety. A holonomic module has $\dim \mathrm{Char}(M) = \dim X$ — neither more nor less.

questions.q: On $X = \mathbb{C}^*$, the rank-1 $\mathcal{D}$-module $M_\alpha = \mathcal{O} \cdot z^\alpha$ has $\nabla(z^\alpha) = \alpha z^{\alpha - 1} dz$. Under the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence, what is the corresponding local system?
choices: Rank $1$, monodromy $e^{2\pi i \alpha}$ around the puncture.
questions.explain: Horizontal sections of $\nabla$ on a small simply connected open are spanned by $z^\alpha$ — this is the unique (up to scalar) flat section. Continue analytically once around $0$: $z^\alpha \mapsto e^{2\pi i \alpha} z^\alpha$, since the branch of $\log z$ acquires $2\pi i$ along the loop. So the monodromy operator on the fibre is multiplication by $e^{2\pi i \alpha}$. When $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}$ this is trivial — and indeed $z^\alpha$ is then a single-valued function, $M_\alpha \cong \mathcal{O}$ as $\mathcal{D}$-modules.
questions.hint: Continue $z^\alpha$ analytically once around $0$. The branch of $\log z$ changes by $2\pi i$.

questions.q: The Riemann-Hilbert correspondence specifically requires REGULAR holonomic D-modules. Why is regularity essential?
choices: Because irregular modules are infinite-dimensional and cannot be matched to perverse sheaves.

Because the de Rham functor still works on irregular modules, but loses information: e.g. $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^*} \cdot e^{1/z}$ has trivial topological monodromy yet is non-trivial as a $\mathcal{D}$-module.
Because perverse sheaves are not defined for irregular monodromy data.
Because regularity is automatic for holonomic D-modules — the qualifier is redundant.
questions.explain: The module $M = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^*} \cdot e^{1/z}$ is holonomic but irregular at $0$: $\nabla(e^{1/z}) = -z^{-2} e^{1/z} dz$ has a pole of order $2$, beyond simple. Its monodromy local system on $\mathbb{C}^*$ is trivial (the multivalued $e^{1/z}$ is single-valued), so the de Rham functor sends $M$ to the same perverse sheaf as $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^*}$ — but $M \not\cong \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^*}$ as $\mathcal{D}$-modules. The 'irregular type' (Stokes data at $0$) is invisible to topology. Regular RH (Kashiwara-Mebkhout) handles regular holonomic; the irregular RH (D'Agnolo-Kashiwara 2016) requires enhanced perverse sheaves to recover Stokes data.
questions.hint: Consider the module $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^*} \cdot e^{1/z}$. What is its topological monodromy, and what do you lose by the de Rham functor?

questions.q: On a smooth variety $X$, the simplest case of the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence is the equivalence between which two categories?
choices: Vector bundles on $X$ and étale local systems on $X$.
Vector bundles with flat connection on $X$ and complex local systems on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$.
All quasi-coherent $\mathcal{D}_X$-modules and all sheaves on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$.
questions.explain:
When $M$ is $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent (a vector bundle) with flat connection $
abla$, the de Rham functor $\mathrm{DR}_X(M) = \Omega^ ullet \otimes^L_{\mathcal{D}_X} M[\dim X]$ collapses to the kernel sheaf $M^
abla$ of horizontal sections (placed in the appropriate degree by the shift). $M^
abla$ is a rank-$\mathrm{rk}(M)$ local system on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and the resulting equivalence — Deligne 1970, refining Hilbert's 21st — was the model for Kashiwara-Mebkhout's general theorem. The general case adds singular perverse sheaves on the topological side and conormal-supported D-modules on the algebraic side.
questions.hint: Specialise to $\mathcal{O}_X$-coherent D-modules. What does the de Rham functor compute then?

questions.q: The Gauss hypergeometric ODE $z(1-z)u'' + (c - (a+b+1)z)u' - abu = 0$ has indicial roots at $z = 0$ given by $\rho \in \{0, 1 - c\}$. The corresponding monodromy eigenvalues at $z = 0$ are then:
questions.explain: Near a regular singular point with indicial roots $\rho_1, \rho_2$, the local solution basis is $\{z^{\rho_1}, z^{\rho_2}\}$ (modulo $\log z$ corrections when $\rho_1 - \rho_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$). Going around the puncture once sends $z^\rho \mapsto e^{2\pi i \rho} z^\rho$, so the monodromy eigenvalues at $z = 0$ are $e^{2\pi i \cdot 0} = 1$ and $e^{2\pi i (1 - c)}$. Same recipe at $z = 1$ (indicial roots $0, c - a - b$) and $z = \infty$ (indicial roots $a, b$).
questions.hint: Indicial roots are the exponents in $z^\rho$ local solutions. Monodromy of $z^\rho$ is $e^{2\pi i \rho}$.

questions.q: The hypergeometric local system on $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, 1, \infty\}$ has rank 2. Why does this match the order of the hypergeometric ODE rather than its degree as a polynomial in $z$?
choices: Coincidence — the rank could be anything.

Because for a holonomic $\mathcal{D}$-module on a smooth curve $U$, the rank of the corresponding local system equals the generic rank of the underlying $\mathcal{O}_U$-module, which for a cyclic module $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D} P$ equals $\mathrm{ord}(P)$.
Because the local system has rank equal to the number of singular points, namely $3 - 1 = 2$.
Because the rank is the dimension of $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, 1, \infty\}$, namely $2$.
questions.explain: On a smooth open curve $U$, a single linear ODE $P u = 0$ of order $n$ has solution space (locally on a simply connected open) of dimension $n$ — the existence-uniqueness theorem for ODEs in the holomorphic category. So the corresponding $\mathcal{D}_U$-module $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}P$ has rank $n$ as $\mathcal{O}_U$-module, and the local system $\mathrm{DR}_U(\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}P)$ has rank $n$. For Gauss hypergeometric, $\mathrm{ord}(P) = 2$, hence rank-$2$ local system, hence monodromy in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{C})$.
questions.hint: On a smooth curve, the rank of a $\mathcal{D}$-module $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}P$ as an $\mathcal{O}$-module is the order of $P$ — the existence-uniqueness theorem for ODEs gives this.

questions.q: What is the fundamental group of $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \setminus \{0, 1, \infty\}$?
choices: Free of rank $2$ (generated by loops around any two of the three punctures).
questions.explain: $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ is simply connected; removing three points gives a free group on two generators (the three loops $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \gamma_\infty$ around the punctures satisfy the single relation $\gamma_0 \gamma_1 \gamma_\infty = 1$). General principle: removing $n$ points from $\mathbb{P}^1$ leaves $\pi_1$ free of rank $n - 1$. So a hypergeometric monodromy representation is a homomorphism $F_2 \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ — pick the images of two generators freely, and the third is determined.
questions.hint: Removing $n$ points from a simply-connected closed surface gives a free group on $n - 1$ generators.

questions.q: Let $f = x \in \mathbb{C}[x]$. What is the Bernstein-Sato polynomial $b_f(s)$, and what is the operator $P(s)$ in the functional equation $P(s) f^{s+1} = b_f(s) f^s$?
questions.explain: Compute: $\partial \cdot x^{s+1} = (s+1) x^s$, so the functional equation $\partial \cdot f^{s+1} = (s+1) f^s$ holds with $P(s) = \partial$ and $b(s) = s + 1$. To see $b_f$ is monic of minimal degree: the relation $f^s \in D[s] \cdot f^{s+1}$ requires at least one application of $\partial$, so the polynomial in $s$ must vanish at $s = -1$ (where $f^{-1+1} = f^0 = 1$ and $f^0 = 1$ but the operator must produce a polynomial, forcing the $(s+1)$ factor). Hence $b_f(s) = s + 1$.

questions.q: Kashiwara's theorem says all roots of $b_f(s)$ are negative rational numbers. For $f = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ (a non-degenerate quadratic in $2$ variables), $b_f(s) = (s + 1)(s + n/2)$ with $n = 2$. What are the roots, and how do they reflect the singularity?
choices: Roots: $-1, -1$. Both at $-1$, reflecting the smooth-point limit.
Roots: $-1, 0$. The root $0$ marks a non-singular germ.
Roots: $-1, -1$. The doubled root reflects $\{f = 0\}$ being a node (two transverse smooth branches).
questions.explain: $b_f(s) = (s + 1)(s + n/2) = (s + 1)^2$ when $n = 2$, with the doubled root at $s = -1$. The location of the largest root tracks the log canonical threshold: $\mathrm{lct}(0; \{f = 0\}) = -\max\{\text{roots}\} = 1$, agreeing with the elementary fact that a node has lct $1$. The multiplicity of the root carries finer information about the Hodge filtration on the vanishing cohomology. (Note: in Kashiwara-Saito's normalisation, all roots of the reduced $b$-function, $b_f(s)/(s+1)$, lie in $(-1, 0)$ — the 'spectrum' — for an isolated singularity.)
questions.hint: Substitute $n = 2$ and read off. Then recall: the largest (least negative) root of $b_f(-s)$ controls $\mathrm{lct}$.

questions.q: Why does the existence of a Bernstein-Sato polynomial follow from holonomicity of $D_n[s] \cdot f^s$?
choices: Because every holonomic D-module over a Noetherian base has finite length, forcing an algebraic relation among $f^s, f^{s-1}, f^{s-2}, \ldots$ that becomes the functional equation after rearrangement.
Because every holonomic D-module is a direct sum of simple ones, and one can take the product of their characters to get $b_f(s)$.
Because Kashiwara's theorem gives an explicit formula for $b_f$.
Because $f^s$ is integral over $\mathbb{C}[s]$ for any $f$.
questions.explain: Bernstein's argument: the module $N = D_n[s] \cdot f^s \subset \mathbb{C}[x, s, f^{-1}] \cdot f^s$ is holonomic over $D_n[s]$ (Bernstein's inequality, applied to the larger ring). Holonomic modules over a Noetherian ring have finite length. Hence the descending chain of submodules $N \supset f \cdot N \supset f^2 \cdot N \supset \cdots$ must stabilise, giving an inclusion $f^k \cdot N \subset f^{k+1} \cdot N$ for some $k$, which translates (after reindexing $s \mapsto s - k$) to a polynomial $b(s)$ with $b(s) f^s \in D_n[s] \cdot f^{s+1}$. The minimal monic such $b$ is $b_f(s)$.
questions.hint: Holonomic ⇒ finite length. What does finite length imply for the chain $N \supset f \cdot N \supset f^2 \cdot N \supset \cdots$?
